title: Three excellences, three cults: latria for God, civil honor for natural dignity, dulia for supernatural grace and glory
source_text: II. Secundo observant tot esse species cultus, sive honoris, quot sunt species excellentiae: quoniam honor, sive cultus debetur personae propter excellentiam. Sed quod ad praesens institutum attinet, tres esse species excellentiae. Prima est excellentia divina & infinita, cui respondet prima species cultus, quae ab Ecclesiae Romanae Theologis Latria dicitur. Secunda est excellentia humana, seu naturalis, quae posita est in humanis virtutibus, dignitatibus, gradibus, &c. Cui respondet secunda species cultus, quae dici potest cultus civilis, & observantia quaedam humana. Tertia est excellentia quaedam media inter divinam & humanam, qualis est gratia & gloria Sanctorum, quae dona sunt supernaturalia; & huic respondet tertia species cultus, quae in Schola Romana Dulia appellatur.
pass_a_gloss: Second, they observe that there are as many species of cult, or honor, as there are species of excellence: because honor, or cult, is owed to a person on account of excellence. But as pertains to the present design, there are three species of excellence. The first is divine and infinite excellence, to which responds the first species of cult, which by the Theologians of the Roman Church is called Latria. The second is human, or natural, excellence, which is placed in human virtues, dignities, grades, etc. To which responds the second species of cult, which can be called civil cult, and a certain human observance. The third is a certain excellence midway between the divine and the human, such as is the grace and glory of the Saints, which are supernatural gifts; and to this responds the third species of cult, which in the Roman School is called Dulia.
pass_b_english: Cult species track excellence species—three for this debate.
Latria answers infinite divine excellence; civil observance answers natural human dignity.
Dulia answers the mid-rank supernatural grace and glory of the Saints.

choices.why: Between divine infinity and mere natural dignity.
